title: The Hanseatic League
context:
Between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries, a network of north European trading towns known as the Hanseatic League dominated commerce across the Baltic and North Seas. It was never a state, and it had no capital, army or permanent officials. Instead, merchants from towns such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Danzig cooperated through shared rules, meeting occasionally at assemblies called diets to settle disputes and agree on common policy. At its height the League included well over a hundred towns.

The goods it carried were bulky and ordinary rather than luxurious. Timber, grain, furs and wax travelled west from the Baltic, while cloth and wine moved east. The most profitable single commodity was salted herring, which was essential for the many fast days of the medieval Christian calendar. Salt from Lüneburg was used to preserve the fish, and Lübeck's control of the salt route gave it a unique advantage over rival ports. Historians estimate that herring made up a large share of Lübeck's income, though precise figures are not available for most years.

Merchants abroad lived in fortified compounds called kontors, the most famous being the Steelyard in London and Bryggen in Bergen. Residents of these compounds were forbidden to marry local women and had to follow strict rules about trade, while young apprentices endured demanding initiation rituals. The compounds were privileged but resented by local traders, who complained that foreigners were taking profits out of the country. Occasionally this resentment turned violent. Life inside the compounds was also tightly regulated in everyday matters: the merchants ate together, locked the gates at night and kept their goods and records inside the walls. The arrangement protected them from theft and local disputes, but it also kept them apart from the towns in which they worked for decades, which did little to improve relations.

The League's power rested on collective action. When a ruler threatened its privileges, member towns could impose a trade embargo, refusing to supply goods until demands were met. In the 1360s the Danish king Valdemar attacked the island town of Visby; the towns responded by forming an alliance and, after a war, forced the king to sign the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370, which confirmed trading rights and gave the League a say in the Danish succession. Historians often regard this as the League's greatest triumph.

Decline came slowly. From the late fifteenth century, the Dutch developed larger, cheaper ships and offered competing services, while stronger national governments in England and Sweden wanted to keep trade profits for their own merchants. The discovery of Atlantic routes shifted the centre of European commerce westward. Although the last formal diet was held in 1669, only three towns attended. Today the heritage is still a matter of civic pride: Hamburg and Bremen continue to describe themselves officially as Hanseatic cities.
